## Animations

Each animation below illustrates Legendre polynomials $P_n(x)$ on $[-1,1]$. The first animation reveals $P_0$ through $P_5$ one per frame; the second shows the Legendre series partial sums converging to $f(x) = e^{x}\cos(\pi x/2)$.

Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

### Case 1 — Successive polynomials $P_0, P_1, \ldots, P_5$

**Properties:** Each $P_n$ is orthogonal to all lower-degree Legendre polynomials on $[-1,1]$. $P_n(1)=1$, $P_n(-1)=(-1)^n$, and $P_n$ has exactly $n$ zeros in $(-1,1)$. They are computed by the recurrence $(n+1)P_{n+1} = (2n+1)xP_n - nP_{n-1}$.

[Julia source](legendrepolyaa.jl)

![Legendre polynomials P_0 through P_5 added one per frame on the interval [-1, 1], showing their oscillatory character](legendrepolyaa.gif)

### Case 2 — Legendre series for $f(x) = e^{x}\cos(\pi x/2)$

**Behavior:** The partial sum $S_N(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} c_n P_n(x)$ with $c_n = \tfrac{2n+1}{2}\int_{-1}^{1} f(x)P_n(x)\,dx$ converges to $f$ as $N\to\infty$. This $f$ is the function of Mathews' Example 8(b); it is neither even nor odd, and every coefficient $c_0, \ldots, c_8$ is nonzero, so each frame adds a new term. Because $S_N$ minimises the integrated squared error rather than the maximum error, the max error need not fall at every step: it rises from 0.699 for $S_0$ to 1.09 for $S_1$, then falls with each added term to $7.74\times 10^{-6}$ for $S_8$.

[Julia source](legendrepolybb.jl)

![Legendre series partial sums S_0 through S_8 for e^x cos(pi x/2), one per frame; every coefficient is nonzero, and the max error rises from 0.699 for S_0 to 1.09 for S_1, then falls with each added term to 7.74e-6 for S_8](legendrepolybb.gif)
